title: Asalha, the fifth time
hookLine: the first sermon, and the rains retreat ahead
tomorrow: who comes back to the old house once a year?

cards: Rain on the windshield, a storm alert on the phone, plans quietly canceled: some seasons tell everyone to stay in. In the Buddha's India, the monsoon did that to the roads. His monks kept walking anyway.
And the neighbors started grumbling. The Vinaya, the monks' rulebook, keeps their complaint: these monks tramp around in the rains, crushing green shoots and the small creatures in them.
Even the birds, people said, build nests in the treetops and stay put. The complaint reached the Buddha, a teacher who walked from town to town himself. What would he do with it?

teach.h: STAY IN ONE PLACE FOR THE RAINS.
teach.b: He listened. He told the monks to stay in one place for the rains. That's vassa, the rains retreat, and the Vinaya starts it the day after the Asalha full moon, the night tradition remembers as the first sermon.
The rule came years after the sermon, but the calendar sets the two side by side.

teach.h: THE WHEEL SET ROLLING AT THE DEER PARK.
teach.b: On the full moon, the wheel is set rolling: at the Deer Park, the Buddha teaches his five old companions about suffering, its cause, its ending and the path.
In the sutta a cry goes up from the earth to the heavens: the wheel has been set rolling, and no one in the world can turn it back.

teach.h: THE WALKING STOPS, THE PRACTICE STAYS.
teach.b: Then, on the calendar, the next morning, the walking stops. One way to read that pairing: the teaching wasn't kept by rushing everywhere.
It was kept by monks who stopped, stayed in one place through the wet months, and practiced.
Monks in Theravada monasteries still keep the rains in one place, and some lay people choose a practice for the season: the precepts on holy days, a drink given up, an extra morning at the temple.
The odd part to pass on tonight: the rains retreat began with neighbors upset about trampled plants.
Five Asalhas on this path, and the sermon still starts again each year, with someone choosing to sit still and look.

how: On the Asalha full moon Theravada Buddhists remember the first sermon at the temple; the next day monks begin the rains retreat in one monastery, and some lay people take on a practice for the season, such as keeping the precepts on holy days.

games.q: you're the Buddha. the neighbors say your monks trample the young plants in the rains, and even the birds stay home. what do you do?
o: tell the monks to stay in one place for the rains.
keep walking; the teaching matters more than plants.
tell the monks to walk only at night, out of sight.
games.why: he listened to the complaint and made the rains retreat. the walking stopped, and the practice stayed.

practice: Choose one practice for the rains, the season ahead: small enough to keep on an ordinary Tuesday. Name what you hope it gives you, the one thing most likely to get in its way, and what you'll do when that happens.
Then sit with your choice, settled, like a monk who has stopped walking.

wordCard.voice: Asalha: the full moon of the first sermon, and the night before the rains retreat begins.

orig.note: Sanskrit name of the month; in Pali it's Asalha, whose full moon remembers the first sermon.

carryVoice: Carry this: the wheel still turns, each time someone stays put long enough to see. Two of seven in the festival year.
